rendered:
The review says the biological process of tumor metastasis primarily involves five critical steps[1] (shown in Fig. 1[2]):

1. local invasion at the primary tumor site[3]. Tumor cells gain stem-cell traits and the ability to invade through epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), which lets them break away from the primary site.
2.[4] intravasation into the circulatory system[5]. Blood vessels formed by cancer cells are often incomplete, highly tortuous and leaky, which makes this possible.
3.[6] survival in circulation[7]. Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) protect themselves by binding to platelets and forming tumor emboli. This helps them withstand shear forces in the bloodstream and avoid attack by natural killer (NK) cells.
4.[8] extravasation into distant organs[9]. CTCs cross the vessel walls of distant organs and enter the tissue, which sets up colonization there.
5.[10] colonization through adaptation to the new microenvironment[11]. Most tumor cells that get through the vessel wall become dormant and avoid immune clearance. They only start growing again when the distant microenvironment is remodeled, often through inflammatory signals or myeloid-derived suppressor cells. That growth produces deadly macro-metastases.

There is an inconsistency in the figure caption. It says the process[12] mainly includes five key steps: intravasation, survival in circulation, extravasation, and colonization and growth[13], but that list leaves out local invasion, so it names fewer steps than it claims.
